newsitem.title: USA: US Air, Continental post mixed results; TWA has loss.
newsitem.headline: US Air, Continental post mixed results; TWA has loss.

text.p: Trans World Airlines Inc. posted a surprisingly big loss for the second quarter Wednesday, while both US Airways Group Inc. and Continental Airlines Inc. did better than Wall Street had anticipated.
US Airways, the nation's sixth-largest carrier, said earnings edged up 2 percent in the quarter.
No. 5 carrier Continental said that while pre-tax earnings set a record in the quarter, net income fell 23 percent. But the results still came in a bit better than expected.
The results lagged those of the parent companies of United Airlines, the nation's largest carrier, and No. 2 American Airlines, both of which reported better-than-expected results for the quarter.

US Airways, based in Airlington, Va., said net income rose to $206 million in the quarter from $201 million a year earlier. Passenger traffic rose 9 percent, its planes ran with more seats filled and average costs fell, the airline said.
Results for the latest quarter included one-time expenses of $28.3 million related to a restructuring.
The earnings came in a few cents above analysts' estimates, according to forecasts tabulated by First Call.

But US Airways' stock lost 75 cents to $38.125 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange since the results fell short of the most optimistic Wall Street expectations, even though it beat average forecasts.
"People had expected a surprise of similar magnitude as seen in the first quarter, and they may have been a little disappointed," said Timothy Ross, an airline analyst with SBC Warburg.

The airline also said it expected to reach a labour agreement with its pilots after making a new offer in contract talks last week. The airline's disputes with union employees have hampered its efforts to compete with other carriers.
The company has promised the union that the airline will grow at the same rate as its rivals, instead of cutting back operations as it has done for the past six years.
The pilots' union said it was "intrigued" by the company's latest offer but it was disappointed that the proposal would not allow the company to expand until 1999 or later.
Sales edged up to $2.2 billion from $2.1 billion.
Continental, based in Houston, said pretax profits of $208 million were the best in its history, but that higher expenses and interest payments reduced net income.

The company said the strong pretax earnings came despite a ticket tax reimposed during the latest quarter, and higher fuel prices partly offset by productivity savings and lower aircraft ownership costs.
Net earnings fell 23 percent to $128 million, or $2.01 a share, from $167 million, or $2.53 a share, a year earlier. Sales rose 9 percent to $1.79 billion from $1.64 billion.
The results beat expectations and Continental's class A stock edged up 37.5 cents to $36, also on the NYSE.

TWA, still struggling to return to financial health a year after the crash of Flight 800, said operating income tumbled 90 percent in the quarter as passenger traffic fell 9 percent, average fares edged lower and operating expenses rose.

The nation's seventh-largest airline reported a loss of $12 million, or 31 cents a share, for the quarter before a one-time charge, compared with a profit of $25.3 million, or 46 cents a share, a year earlier.
Analysts had forecast TWA would lose 23 cents a share before special items, according to First Call, and TWA stock lost 31 cents to $6.31 on the NYSE.

The carrier's cash position continued to dwindle, falling to about $103 million as of June 30 from $182 million at the end of 1996. Industry analysts said last week that time may be running out for the once-proud airline.
